title: The Lowest Tide
subtitle: Friday 17 to Wednesday 29 October 1924: A Keeper's Father's Log, a Minister's Letter, Forty Sticks of Dynamite, and One Hour on the Church Shelf

setting.name: Carrow Island and Rockland, the dark of the moon, October 1924
setting.description: Between the spring tides there is no ringing, and for ten days the island breathes. The party have time to dig: on the mainland, in the Rockland Mariner's files for 1871, the Knox County probate records, and the writing desk of the last of the Vinings; on the island, in Oren Pinkham's father's logbook, Galen Coombs's business, and the Captain's House. Then, from Sunday 26 October, a hard northwest gale blows for three days, driving the water out of Penobscot Bay, the moon goes new on the 28th with the moon near perigee, and every low water is lower than the last. On Wednesday 29 October, at 5:48 a.m., in the dark before dawn, comes the lowest tide anyone on the Maine coast has seen: the Church Shelf bare, and the drowned Union Church of 1858 standing out of the sea in a pool of black water, for one hour. Orpha Sprague has warned the party that on that tide the bell will call every one of the five families' blood at once, sixty-one grown men and women on Carrow. Galen Coombs means to be out on the Shelf with his crew, to recover the cargo he has sunk in the church and to blow the church to pieces with forty sticks of dynamite. The doors are still spiked shut. Behind them, Ardelia Vining is still ringing.
setting.atmosphere: Ten days of clear cold October weather, the bay hard blue, the maples on the mainland hills red, the island splitting wood and banking houses with spruce boughs for the winter; then the gale, a roaring dry northwest wind that never stops for three days, that strips the last leaves, slams doors, and pulls the sea out of the harbor until the boats lie on their sides in the mud and old men walk out onto ledges they have never seen above water. The set piece is darkness, cold, wet stone, weed, the smell of the sea bottom, lantern light on green slime, the sound of water draining everywhere at once, and then the bell, in the open air, for the first time since 1871: enormous. Dread rises through the act as the water falls. Then the hour on the Shelf is pure dread and action: get in, open the doors, get everyone out, before the sea comes home.

keyLocations.name: Rockland: the Mariner's files, the probate court and Miss Vining's parlor
keyLocations.description: The mainland, by the Wednesday or Friday mail boat (back on the next run, two days later). Rockland in 1924 is a working port of eight thousand people: lime kilns smoking along the shore, sardine factories, schooners loading granite and lime, the Knox County courthouse on the hill, a Main Street of brick blocks, the Thorndike Hotel, and the office of the Rockland Mariner, a weekly since 1846, whose bound files fill a back room. On Middle Street, in a narrow yellow house full of clocks, lives Miss Prudence Vining, seventy-nine, retired schoolmistress, the Reverend Joel Vining's niece.
features: The Mariner's bound volume for 1871 and 1872, foxed and smelling of mice
The Knox County probate court's docket books for 1871 to 1874, in the courthouse basement
Miss Vining's writing desk, a lap desk of rosewood, and a packet of letters tied with black ribbon
encounters: The Mariner's elderly file clerk, Willard Hosmer, who has been waiting forty years for someone to ask about something interesting
Miss Prudence Vining, who has waited fifty-two years to be asked about her uncle, and will not hand over his letters to anyone who laughs
secrets: CLUE D7 (core, the Mariner's file, 9 November 1871; Research DC 10 to find in an hour, automatic in a day): a letter from the owners of the schooner Hannah Leighton of Gloucester: 'We are informed that six of our crew, put ashore sick at Carrow Island, were lost in the gale of the 18th inst. in a meeting house on a point exposed to the sea. We ask the selectmen of Carrow why sick seamen were lodged in such a place in such weather, and why, as we are told, no boat put off.' No reply was printed. The crew's six names are listed (CLUE F4: Staples, Hamor, Joyce, Pert, Torrey, Dunbar).

The Mariner of 26 October 1871 (automatic, beside D7): 'GALE AT CARROW. The Point meeting house carried away with all who had sheltered there, being twenty-three souls, many of them sick of the fever then prevailing. The selectmen report that every effort was made.' Seventeen of the twenty-three names are printed, from the Proprietors' list.

The probate dockets (Research DC 14, or an Educated character's Seen It in a Book): between December 1871 and 1874 the leases, net stands, flake yards and fishing privileges of eleven Point households 'whose holders are deceased' pass to Hezekiah Sprague, Seth Wyman, Jabez Coombs, Reuben Farr and Eliphalet Tibbetts, for unpaid rents. Mattie Grindle's great-grandfather's privilege went to Hezekiah Sprague. This is not a clue to a rule; it is what the island has been living on.

CLUE A5, E5 and F2 (core, Miss Vining's packet; she will read it aloud, or lend it to anyone who treats it, and her, with respect; Persuasion DC 12 or Imogen's Folklorist tradition or Kingsley Trask's collar): the Reverend Joel Vining's letter to his brother Amos, Bangor, March 1872. 'I came home to find my wife drowned and the island's selectmen saying she sheltered. She did not shelter. She went in to nurse the sick of the Point, and they shut the doors on her and the sick together and nailed them with iron, and in the gale they stood on the Bar with lanterns and let the sea have the church, because of the fever. Orpha Sprague told me, and her father held the lantern she held. I have no proof that a court would take. And now the old bell rings under the sea at the bottom of the great tides, and calls the men who did it home by their names, and their brothers and their sons; it took Asahel Wyman in November. I have found it can be answered: ring a bell by hand from the land while it rings, and it is quiet for that tide, as though someone had come. They could not pass the iron, God help them, and so they cannot pass it now. I believe she will be quiet for good only when the doors they spiked are opened from without, and one of their own blood rings for each of them by name before all the island, so that the island owns what it did. I cannot make them do it. I have left money for the ringing. God forgive me, I am going away.'

keyLocations.name: Carrow Head Light: the watch room and the 1871 logbook
keyLocations.description: The watch room at the top of the iron tower, under the lantern: a desk, a stove, a chair, the logbooks on their shelf, the barometer, the station telescope on its bracket at the window looking south over the Bar and the Shelf. Oren Pinkham's father's volume for 1871 is wrapped in oilcloth at the back of the shelf.
features: Nehemiah Pinkham's logbook for 1871, in a neat Cape Elizabeth hand, the entry for 18 and 19 October underlined twice in a different ink
The barometer, which Oren taps every hour from Sunday 26 October and does not like
The almanac and the Coast Survey tide tables, with Oren's sums in the margin
encounters: Oren Pinkham, who has decided, and puts the book on the table and says nothing at all
secrets: CLUE D1 (core; Oren shows it when the party ask him honestly after a life has been saved, or when the GM needs it: see controlFile.theKeyClue): 'Oct. 18, 1871. Wind S.E., heavy gale, rain, high sea. 10.30 p.m. Sea breaking over the Bar. 11 p.m. Bell at Point meeting house rung, and continued. Five lanterns on the Bar. Selectmen's watch. No boat put off. Watched until 3.40 a.m. when bell ceased. At daylight meeting house gone. Twenty-three were in it, shut there by order of the selectmen on account of the fever. I could have launched the station boat and did not, being told it was not my business. God forgive this island. God forgive me. N. Pinkham, Keeper.'

Oren's sums (automatic once he has done them on Sunday 26 October, or Nature DC 14 for anyone with the almanac and the barometer): the moon new on the 28th and near its perigee; a gale out of the northwest blowing the bay empty; the dawn low water on Wednesday 29 October at 5:48 a.m. will be four or five feet below any he has logged. 'The Shelf'll be dry. The old church'll be standing in the open. For about an hour, from a quarter past five, and then she'll come back fast, because the wind's going to drop and back round before daylight. You'll have till about quarter past six.'

From the gallery with the telescope at Tuesday 28 October's dawn low water (Perception DC 10): the drowned church's tower and the ridge of its roof breaking the surface of the sea for the first time since 1871, black with weed, and on it, standing in the water up to its waist, a figure that is not there when you lower the glass. Fear check DC 15.

keyLocations.name: Sculpin Cove
keyLocations.description: Galen Coombs's place on the north shore: a fish house on pilings with a loft, a stone wharf, a marine railway with the Lark's Daughter hauled up on it, the Ruth & Ida at her mooring, a shed of salvage gear (a hand-pumped air compressor, a copper diving helmet and canvas dress, lead boots, two hundred feet of hose), and a stove where twenty young island men play cards and wait for dark. A good place for a party with Galen's trust, and a very bad one for a party without it.
features: The salvage shed: the deep-sea dress, the air pump, grapnels, salt sacks and burlap
Galen's chart of the south shore, pinned on the fish house wall, with the Shelf hatched in pencil, the church marked with an X, and two buoys
A wooden box marked WEIR STAKES under the loft ladder, forty sticks of dynamite inside, and a coil of fuse; the caps are in a cigar box on the shelf
encounters: Galen Coombs and eight to twelve of his crew (Night Watchman statistics), at cards, at work on the boats, or at the Grange dance on Saturday 25 October
Arno Farr, Galen's diver, who has been inside the drowned church in the dress three times this summer and will not go again
secrets: CLUE H1 (core, from Captain Stinson's freight book or the Rockland hardware dealer, or seen in the shed): forty sticks of forty-per-cent dynamite and a hundred feet of fuse, shipped on the mail boat on 22 October, consigned to 'G. Coombs, weir stakes'. The blasting caps came from Peleg Sprague, from the old quarry stores, in September.

CLUE H2 (core, the Grange dance on Saturday 25 October, behind the hall, or the fish house stove; anyone with Standing 0 or better who drinks with the crew): 'Galen says the big tide'll settle it. The bell and the cargo both. We go out at four, bring up the sacks, set the charge on the church wall, and light out. Says he'll not wait to be called like Aunt Sophie.'

CLUE H3 (core, the chart on the fish house wall, or the Light's telescope): the X on the church and two buoys marking the salt-sack cache on the Shelf's edge; and in Galen's hand beside it, 'west wall, 8 sticks, door side'. Galen means to bring the wall down on the doors.

Arno Farr's story (Insight DC 12 to see he wants to tell it; whisky helps): 'Galen sends me down in the dress in July to sink the sacks inside, where the Coast Guard can't grapple 'em. Through the vestry window, it's broke. Inside, it's pews. There's people in the pews, mister. Old ones and new. Enoch Farr's in the third pew in his oilskins. And the doors are nailed. From outside. Big iron spikes, eight of 'em. Who nails a church shut from outside? And there's a woman in the porch holding the bell rope. She looked at me. I come up and I told Galen I'm done.' (A half-clue to D3 and to Ardelia; core clue E2 confirmation for later.)

CLUE H4 (Galen himself, to anyone of the blood who drinks with him, or to Peg Tolman): 'It's a curse my great-great-grandfather bought and I'm done paying. I'll put it back in the sea where it came from. Forty sticks. Nobody else needs to walk.' He does not know what the doors mean. If told (with D1 or Vining's letter), he does not believe it until he sees the spikes.

keyLocations.name: The Church Shelf and the drowned church
keyLocations.description: Beyond the end of Church Point the sea floor drops in a clay slope to the Shelf, a broad tilted ledge of granite three hundred yards long, which at an ordinary low water lies under eight feet of water and on Wednesday 29 October lies bare. In the middle of it, settled at an angle on the stone where it slid in 1871, stands the Union Church of 1858: a white clapboard meeting house forty feet by sixty, its roof broken in along one side, its square tower leaning toward the Point, everything black and green with weed, barnacle and mussel, every window boarded from outside with planks gone soft as cheese, and its double west doors facing the island, shut. The Shelf is slick weed, pools, kelp, the wreck of a dory, Galen's salt-sacks bobbing in a channel at its seaward edge, and water draining away everywhere with a sound like breathing.
features: The west doors: two heavy panelled leaves under a broken pediment, eight iron spikes as thick as a thumb driven through them into the frame from outside, two iron straps across them, all crusted with rust and shell
The vestibule, reached only through the doors (or by a diver through the vestry window): the bell rope coming down through the ceiling, and the plaster of the walls scratched all over with a nail
The nave: twelve pews each side, silt to the ankles, a pulpit fallen sideways, and in the pews, sitting, shapes
The tower: the bell still in it, tilted in its rotten frame, forty feet above the stone, which in air rings like the end of the world
The vestry: a small room off the chancel with a narrow broken window, and Galen's whisky in salt-sacks stacked to the ceiling
encounters: The called of the five families, walking out across the Shelf in the dark in their nightclothes toward the doors
Galen Coombs's crew, recovering cargo and setting the charge
Ardelia Vining, the Ringer (see Act 3), in the vestibule, on the rope
Drowned Ones: the twenty-three of 1871 and the three of 1924, sitting in the pews, who stand when the doors open
secrets: CLUE D3 (core, automatic for anyone who looks at the doors): spiked shut from outside, with eight iron spikes and two iron straps, and every window boarded from outside. The church was not a shelter. It was a prison.

CLUE D4 and F4 (core, automatic for anyone who enters the vestibule with a light): the plaster is covered with scratched writing, done with a nail, in a dozen hands: names, prayers, 'Lord have mercy', 'water in the porch 10 oclock', 'they will come', and in big uneven capitals at eye height: THEY ARE ON THE BAR WITH LANTERNS. Seventeen of the twenty-three names are legible, each in its own hand; Ardelia Vining's is by the bell rope, small and neat, with 'rang 11 till' and nothing after.

The taken of 1924 (automatic, fear check DC 15; Physician's Clinical Detachment applies to the three, not to the old dead): Enoch Farr in his oilskins in the third pew on the left; Esther Thurlow in her blue coat and stocking feet beside him; Jotham Wyman behind them, his cap on his knee. They are sitting up, as if in church, perfectly preserved by the cold, eyes shut. Of the twenty-three of 1871 there are shapes under the weed and silt in the other pews, and nothing more needs to be said about them. Esther can be carried out (she weighs what she weighed; it takes one strong person five minutes to get her to the Point, under the circumstances); if she, Enoch and Jotham are brought out and buried under their own names, they do not walk in db-scenario-003.

CLUE F3 (the Sensitive's Thin Place or Listener in the vestibule, or anyone who speaks to Ardelia): 'You came. Open the door. Then say who we were. Say it where they can hear. All of them. Every one.'

keyLocations.name: The Captain's House, the night before
keyLocations.description: Tuesday 28 October, after dark, with the gale roaring in the chimneys and the sea gone out of the harbor. Orpha Sprague sends for the party, and for Peleg, and for nobody else.
features: The parlor, the family Bible on its stand, her father's chair, a lamp
The widow's walk, where the wind will take your hat to New Brunswick
encounters: Orpha Sprague, at her most formidable and most frightened
secrets: Orpha tells the party, if they have shown her Vining's letter or Nehemiah Pinkham's log, that it is true. She says only this: 'I held the lantern. I was twenty. My father said no, and I said nothing, and I have said nothing for fifty-three years. Tomorrow it will call every one of us of the blood, and I am going to answer it. I am going out to that door, young man, and I am going to stand there and be what my father would not.' She means it. She cannot be talked out of going; she can be talked into letting someone else open the door while she stands beside it, or locked in, which she will never forgive.
She will not yet give up the order of 9 October 1871 in the Bible. 'After. If there is an after.'

If asked who of the blood is on the island, she knows every one: sixty-one grown men and women, from herself and Lucretia Farr at eighty-four to Peleg and young Frank Wyman, and Dr. Thurlow makes sixty-two. She will write the list if asked, from memory, in a copperplate hand.

synopsis: Ten days of quiet, and then the lowest tide in a hundred years. In Rockland, the Mariner's 1871 files show the island's version of the gale and the Gloucester owners' question, why sick seamen were in a church on a point and why no boat put off; the probate dockets show the Point families' livings passing to the five Proprietors; and the Reverend Joel Vining's niece reads aloud her uncle's 1872 letter, which says plainly that the Proprietors spiked the church shut on the sick and the minister's wife and stood on the Bar with lanterns while the sea took it, explains the bell's rules, and says how it will end. On the island, Oren Pinkham puts his father's logbook on the table, Galen Coombs buys forty sticks of dynamite, and a northwest gale empties the bay. Orpha Sprague tells the party that on the coming tide the bell will call every one of the blood at once, and that she means to answer it. The island tries to lock its sixty-one people of the blood indoors, and some of them get out. At a quarter past five on Wednesday 29 October, in the dark before dawn, the Church Shelf is bare and the drowned church stands in the open air; the bell begins, enormous, and a line of men and women in nightclothes walks out across the weed toward it, Orpha Sprague among them, and Galen Coombs and his crew are already at the west wall with the dynamite. The party have an hour to reach the doors, draw eight iron spikes, keep Galen's charge from bringing the wall down on them, and get everyone off the Shelf before the sea comes home. When the doors open, the bell stops in the middle of a stroke, every one of the called wakes up a long way from shore, and the party see the dead in the pews stand up. That night, on the flood tide, wet footprints come up out of the sea to the doors of the Harbor.
hook: Wednesday 22 October, the Store. The mail boat brings forty sticks of dynamite in a box marked weir stakes, a letter from Merrymeeting Life telling Len Garrity to come home, and Captain Stinson, who stands at the stove a long time and then says to nobody: 'Glass is falling over to Rockland. Wind'll go round northwest Sunday and blow three days. New moon Tuesday. My father used to say a nor'wester on a perigee tide would show you the bottom of the bay.' Then he looks at the party. 'You'll want to ask Oren Pinkham about the bottom of the bay.'

conclusions.conclusion: D. The church doors were spiked shut by the five Proprietors, who stood on the Bar and let the sea take it
clues: D1: Nehemiah Pinkham's 1871 log: five lanterns, no boat put off, 'shut there by order of the selectmen' (the Light)
D7: the Hannah Leighton owners' letter, 'why no boat put off' (the Mariner's files, Rockland)
D3: the doors, spiked from outside, the windows boarded from outside (the Shelf)
D4: the vestibule plaster: THEY ARE ON THE BAR WITH LANTERNS (the drowned church)
Joel Vining's letter: 'they shut the doors on her and the sick together and nailed them with iron' (Miss Vining, Rockland)

conclusions.conclusion: F. It ends when the doors are opened from without and the dead are named and rung for by the five families' blood, before the island (Rule 5)
clues: F1: the ballad's last verse, upside down in Zeb Lunt's ringing book (the church tower)
F2: Joel Vining's letter: 'one of their own blood rings for each of them by name before all the island' (Rockland)
F3: Ardelia Vining herself: 'Say who we were. Say it where they can hear' (the drowned church)
F4: the names, from the plaster, the Mariner's crew list and Zeb's flyleaf (several places)
F5: the doors opened, the call ends, but the bell is not laid (the Shelf)

conclusions.conclusion: H. Galen Coombs means to blow up the drowned church on the lowest tide
clues: H1: the dynamite on the freight book, 'weir stakes' (the mail boat, Sculpin Cove)
H2: his crew's talk at the Grange dance (the Grange hall)
H3: his chart: 'west wall, 8 sticks, door side' (Sculpin Cove, the Light's telescope)

conclusions.conclusion: E. The dead cannot pass iron set by a living hand (Rule 4)
clues: E1: the spikes and horseshoes over every Harbor door, all put up in the spring of 1872 (db-scenario-001)
E5: Joel Vining's letter: 'They could not pass the iron, God help them, and so they cannot pass it now' (Rockland)
D3: the iron spikes and straps held them in the church for fifty-three years (the Shelf)
E2: the wet footprints that come up from the sea on the night of 29 October stop at every door with iron over it (the Harbor, end of the scenario)

acts.title: Ten Days: The Mainland and the Log
acts.description: Friday 17 to Saturday 25 October. No ringing (the tides are neaps); the island is grateful, wary and busy. The party have time to follow every thread: a trip to Rockland on the Wednesday boat for the Mariner's files, the probate court and Miss Prudence Vining; Oren's father's log at the Light; Galen Coombs and Sculpin Cove; Mattie Grindle's grandmother's list; the Captain's House, which is closed again. Len Garrity's company recalls him by letter on the 22nd; whether he goes is a good character moment. Esther Thurlow's notebook leads Dr. Thurlow to the Tibbetts papers; Imogen Lisle can find the last verse in Zeb's book; Pearl Haverty, after the seance, cannot stop hearing the bell rope at night. The answering ringing is now the party's job and the island's, every spring tide; Kingsley Trask asks Peleg and the party to teach the Harbor's young men to ring in shifts.
objectives: Read the island's 1871 story in the Mariner, and the Gloucester owners' question
Get Joel Vining's letter from his niece, and with it Rules 4 and 5
Find out what Galen Coombs means to do with forty sticks of dynamite

scenes.name: Miss Vining's Clocks
scenes.description: Rockland, Middle Street, a narrow yellow house where eleven clocks tick slightly out of time with each other. Miss Prudence Vining, seventy-nine, taught Rockland's grammar school for forty-four years and has never married, and she keeps her uncle Joel's letters in a rosewood lap desk tied with a black ribbon. She has read them a hundred times. Nobody has ever asked her about them, and she suspects anyone who does of wanting to make her uncle a story in a newspaper. She tests them: who are you, why do you want to know, what will you do with it. A party that tells her the truth, that the bell is ringing again and people are walking into the sea, gets the letter read aloud in her dry schoolroom voice, and then lent, with instructions to bring it back. A party that lies to her gets tea and nothing.
scenes.readAloud: The parlor is very small and very clean and full of clocks: a banjo clock, a shelf clock, a tall case clock in the corner, a little brass one under a glass dome, eleven of them, all ticking, none of them quite together, so that the room sounds like rain. Miss Vining sits very upright in a horsehair chair with a rosewood lap desk on her knees and her hands folded on it, and looks at you over her spectacles the way she has looked at forty-four years of Rockland boys who had not done their sums. 'My uncle Joel,' she says, 'was the gentlest man I ever knew. He came to live with us in Bangor in 1873, the year I began teaching, and he never smiled again, and he never once told me why. He told my father, in letters. My father kept them. I have them.' She does not open the desk. 'I should like to know,' she says, 'why I should give my uncle's grief to you.'

skillChecks.success: You tell her the truth, and she believes you, because she has been waiting fifty-two years for someone to tell her this. She unties the ribbon and reads you the letter of March 1872 aloud, steadily, and when she reaches 'God forgive me, I am going away' her voice does not change at all. (CLUES A5, E5, F2; Joel Vining's account of 1871.)
skillChecks.failure: She gives you tea, and asks after the island, and says that her uncle's letters are private, and that if anyone from Carrow wants to read them, they may come and ask her themselves. (Come back with Kingsley Trask, or Orpha Sprague's name, or Mattie Grindle: any of them gets the letter at once.)

skillChecks.success: She knows what is in the letters and has always half believed it. What she wants is not to be told her uncle was a liar or a fool; she wants to be told he was right.
skillChecks.failure: A formidable old schoolmistress who does not like you. That much is clear.

skillChecks.success: It is only a letter, in an old woman's parlor, among clocks. You hold on to that.
skillChecks.failure: They nailed the doors. They stood on the Bar with lanterns and listened to her ring for four hours. You understand, all at once, the whole of it, and what the island has been living on since. Gain 1 Dread (the truth of it; Occultist's Steeped in It and everyone's rule knowledge lower the DC as usual).

scenes.name: Nehemiah Pinkham's Page
scenes.description: The watch room at the Light. Oren Pinkham has decided. He does not say anything. He takes the oilcloth bundle from the back of the shelf, unwraps it on the desk under the lamp, opens it at 18 October 1871 and steps back to the window and looks out at the Bar while the party read it (CLUE D1). Afterwards he says, without turning round, what his father told him in 1890, and what he heard in the bell on 1 August. Then he says, 'Well. Now somebody else knows,' and goes down to make coffee.
scenes.readAloud: The watch room is round and warm, with the great lens turning slowly above your heads and its light going out over the dark water every ten seconds. Oren Pinkham unwraps the oilcloth as if there were something alive in it. The book is a Lighthouse Service logbook like the others, ruled in red, the entries in a small neat hand. He opens it at a page that has been opened a great many times, puts the lamp beside it, and goes and stands at the window with his back to you. Most of the page is wind and weather and oil. The entry for the night of the 18th of October 1871 is underlined twice, in a different ink, as though someone had come back to it years later and could not leave it alone.

skillChecks.success: Oren has carried this for thirty-four years, and his father for fifty before that. He does not want absolution. He wants it to be used.
skillChecks.failure: The old keeper is very quiet. You do not know him well enough to know what it costs.

skillChecks.success: Nehemiah's times match the ringing book and Vining's letter exactly: bell from 11 p.m., ceased 3:40 a.m. And the log for 14 October 1871 has a line nobody has noticed: 'Selectmen sent to station for spikes and straps from the boat house, being short at the works. Gave six.' The keeper's own iron is in those doors.
skillChecks.failure: It says what it says. That is enough.

skillChecks.success: You read it twice and close it, carefully, and put your hand flat on it for a moment as if it might open itself again.
skillChecks.failure: 'No boat put off.' Gain 1 Dread. (A party that has already failed this fear check for Vining's letter does not pay again: it is the same horror.)

scenes.name: Weir Stakes
scenes.description: Sculpin Cove, any evening. Galen Coombs is a host: whisky, a seat at the stove, stories about Rum Row, an offer of work for anyone who can handle a boat or keep their mouth shut. He does not hide his plan from people of the blood; he is proud of it. He thinks the bell is a curse his great-great-grandfather bought from somebody, and that dynamite will end it. He wants his cargo back too: three hundred cases sunk in salt-sacks inside the drowned church, worth $18,000 in Portland. If the party show him the evidence (D1, Vining's letter), he goes very still, and then says he does not believe it, and that even if it is true, a church blown to matchwood can't call anyone. He is wrong (Rule 5: dynamite is the wrong rite; it buries the doors, and the next ringing calls two). He can be talked out of it only by seeing the spikes with his own eyes, or by Orpha Sprague, or by force. A party that tells the Coast Guard about the dynamite loses Standing 2 and makes Galen an enemy; the patrol boat will not come out in the gale anyway.
scenes.readAloud: The fish house at Sculpin Cove is a long dim room over the water with a stove at one end, nets hung from the rafters, a card table under a lantern, and twelve young men who stop talking when you come in. Galen Coombs gets up from the table and comes to meet you with his hand out and a glass in it. 'Peg's friends,' he says. 'Or the minister's. Or the insurance man's. On this island you have to be somebody's. Sit down.' Behind him, on the wall, is a chart of the south shore with the Shelf hatched in pencil and an X in the middle of it, and under the loft ladder, half covered by a tarpaulin, a pine box stencilled WEIR STAKES. Galen sees you see it, and grins, with a gold tooth. 'That,' he says, 'is how this island stops walking into the sea.'

skillChecks.success: Galen listens. He does not agree, but he agrees to wait: he will not light the fuse until the party have had their go at the doors, and he will bring his crew to help pull the called off the Shelf. (Showing him D1 or Vining's letter gives advantage; Peg Tolman, who has his respect, gives advantage; Orpha Sprague's word makes it automatic.)
skillChecks.failure: 'You've been talking to the minister.' He is cheerful, generous and immovable. He will set the charge at half past five on the 29th, whatever anyone says.

skillChecks.success: Late on a dark night you get into the shed and the fish house unseen. You can take the caps from the cigar box, which makes the dynamite useless until Galen finds more (he has six more caps at his house), or wet the fuse, or simply count it and leave.
skillChecks.failure: One of the crew sees you. You are walked to the cove's mouth by four men (Night Watchman statistics) and told, politely, that Galen will want to see you tomorrow. Standing -1 at the Cove.

skillChecks.success: Galen is terrified. Under the grin he is a man who watched his aunt walk into the sea in her nightgown and could not stop her, and who has decided that the only thing he can do is blow something up. He will listen to anyone who offers him something better to do with his hands.
skillChecks.failure: A cheerful rum-runner with a box of dynamite. He seems to think it is all a great joke.

encounters: Willard Hosmer, the Mariner's file clerk, and Miss Prudence Vining: social scenes in Rockland
Galen Coombs's crew (Night Watchman statistics), if the party get on the wrong side of Sculpin Cove; Galen does not want anyone killed and his men fight with fists and boathooks
The Grange dance on Saturday 25 October, the night before the gale: the whole island, a fiddle, and Galen's crew talking (CLUE H2)

acts.title: The Northwest Gale
acts.description: Sunday 26 to Tuesday 28 October. The wind goes into the northwest on Sunday morning and blows a gale for three days, dry, cold and roaring. It pulls the water out of the bay: each low water is lower than the last, the harbor drains to mud and the boats lie on their sides, ledges nobody has seen in living memory show above the water, and on Tuesday at dawn the drowned church's tower breaks the surface off Church Point for the first time since 1871, and the whole island goes down to the shore to look at it. Orpha Sprague sends for the party that night. The island, led by Ellery Wyman and Kingsley Trask, makes its plan: every person of the blood to be locked in a room tonight, with someone not of the blood to keep the key and sit with them until well after daylight. The answering bell to be rung from the church tower by shifts of non-blood men and women. The party are asked to help, and to stand on the Bar in case anyone gets out.
objectives: Learn the hour of the lowest tide and how long the Shelf will be bare
Hear Orpha Sprague's warning, and her intention
Help the island lock in its sixty-one, and plan for those who will get out
Decide who will go out onto the Shelf, with what: crowbars, lanterns, rope, a stretcher, Peleg's Sapper skill

scenes.name: The Bottom of the Bay
scenes.description: Tuesday 28 October, dawn low water, 5:02 a.m. The whole island on the south shore with lanterns, in the roaring wind, watching the sea go out further than anyone has ever seen it go, until, a little after five, the top of a square tower breaks the surface off the end of Church Point, black with weed, and then the ridge of a roof. Nobody speaks. A woman starts to sing a hymn and stops. Use the scene for a long look at what the party will walk into tomorrow: the distance (four hundred yards from the head of the Bar to the church door), the slope from the Point down onto the Shelf, the channels, the pools, where the water will come back first. Oren Pinkham, with his telescope, tells them the rest.
scenes.readAloud: The wind has been blowing for two days and two nights out of the northwest, dry and cold and so hard that you lean on it, and it has been pushing the sea out of the bay like a hand pushing water out of a basin. This morning the harbor is mud from the wharf to the moorings, and the lobster boats lie on their sides in it like dead gulls. The Bar is a causeway as wide as a road. Beyond the end of Church Point, where the land stops, the sea has gone back and back, showing weed and stone and pools, and the whole island is standing on the shore in the dark with lanterns, a hundred people, watching. At four minutes past five somebody says, quietly, 'There.' And out there in the grey, where the water is still dark, something square and black comes up through the surface: the top of a tower, leaning, crusted, streaming water, and behind it, slowly, the long broken ridge of a roof. A woman beside you begins to sing 'Shall We Gather at the River' in a thin voice, and stops after the first line.

skillChecks.success: It is a drowned building on a ledge at low water. You make yourself look at it as Oren does: distances, slopes, footing, time.
skillChecks.failure: It is the church. It is coming up out of the sea, and the people who were nailed into it are still in it. Gain 1 Dread.

skillChecks.success: With the light growing you can see the line you will have to take tomorrow: down the clay slope at the end of the Point, across a hundred yards of slick weed with two channels to wade, to the church's west front. The doors are on this side. You can see the iron straps across them from here.
skillChecks.failure: It is too dark and too far. You will have to find the way tomorrow, in worse light.

skillChecks.success: The wind will drop before dawn tomorrow and back into the south; when it does, all the water it has been holding out of the bay will come home at once, faster than any ordinary flood. Oren says the same, with the hour: 'Quarter past six, she'll be over the Shelf. Half past, over the church floor. You do not want to be on that ledge at twenty past.'
skillChecks.failure: The tide will come back. You do not know how fast. You should ask the keeper.

scenes.name: Orpha Sprague's Lantern
scenes.description: Tuesday night, the Captain's House. Orpha has sent for the party and for Peleg. If they have Vining's letter or Nehemiah's log she confirms it in one sentence. Then she tells them that she is going out tomorrow, and why. Let the party argue. She will not be locked in. She can be persuaded to let someone else open the door while she stands beside it and holds the lantern, as she held one for her father; that is what she wants, in the end, and it is the right ending for this scene. Peleg, white, says he will go too, since he will be called anyway, and he would rather walk out there on his own feet with a crowbar than in a dream. Dr. Thurlow, of the blood, has the same choice.
scenes.readAloud: The wind is screaming round the Captain's House, and every few seconds the whole house shudders and the lamp flame leans. Orpha Sprague sits in her father's chair, which nobody sits in, very small and very straight in black silk, with her hands on the head of a cane and a ship's lantern, old and brass and polished, on the floor beside her feet. 'This was his,' she says. 'I held it on the Bar. I was twenty. He said no, and the others said no, and I said nothing. I have said nothing since.' She looks at each of you in turn. 'Tomorrow morning the sea will go out to the bottom, and she'll ring, and she'll call every one of us of the blood. Sixty-one of us. Sixty-two with the doctor. And I am going to answer. I am going to walk out across the Shelf to that door with this lantern, and stand there, which is what I ought to have done when I was twenty. You can come or not. You cannot stop me.'

skillChecks.success: She agrees to go out with the party, on her own feet, awake, before the bell begins, holding the lantern, and to stand beside the door while someone else draws the spikes. She asks that it be Mattie Grindle, if Mattie will. (If the party suggest it first, no roll is needed.)
skillChecks.failure: She will go alone, at the bell, called like the others, in her nightgown; the party will have to find her on the Shelf.

skillChecks.success: She is not trying to die. She wants to be there when the doors open, and she believes, rightly, that she owes it. She is also very frightened, and will take a hand if someone offers it.
skillChecks.failure: An old woman who has made up her mind. There is nothing in her face to read.

skillChecks.success: Outside the window, at the bottom of the hill, the sea is a long way out, and you can hear it, far off, breathing.
skillChecks.failure: When she says 'sixty-one of us' you think of them all, every one you have met, walking. Gain 1 Dread.

scenes.name: Locking the Island In
scenes.description: Tuesday night, the Harbor. Ellery Wyman and Kingsley Trask organise it at the Store: every one of the blood to be in a locked room by four in the morning, with a keeper not of the blood sitting outside the door, and the answering bell to be rung from the church tower in shifts. It mostly works. The party can help, and should be told what will go wrong: the called have more strength than they should; locks are old; windows are not barred; and some people of the blood do not want to be locked in by their neighbors. Let the party choose where to stand. At the bell, nine of the sixty-one get out: Orpha (unless she is already out with the party), Peleg (unless likewise), Lucretia Farr, eighty-four, through a window; Sophronia Coombs, again; Ellery Wyman, who locked himself in and broke his own door down; four of Galen's crew who refused to be locked in and went out to the Shelf with Galen, and Galen himself.
scenes.readAloud: The Store at ten at night is full of lamplight, smoke, wet oilskins and every grown person on the island, and Ellery Wyman, standing on a cracker box behind the counter with a list in his hand, is reading out names. Who of the blood, and who will keep them, and which room, and which key. Nobody argues. Old men who have not spoken to each other in thirty years agree to sit up together. A Farr wife hands her husband's door key to a Grindle without a word. Kingsley Trask is writing out the ringing shifts on the back of a hymn sheet. And outside, the wind, and under the wind, very far off, the sea going away.

skillChecks.success: You help Ellery and Kingsley make it work: the right keepers on the right doors, ropes as well as locks, two ringers to every shift. Only six of the blood get out at the bell instead of nine (the GM removes Sophronia, Lucretia and one of Galen's crew).
skillChecks.failure: It is done as well as frightened people can do it. Nine will get out.

skillChecks.success: You go round the Harbor with Peleg's tools and nail the windows of the rooms of the blood shut, and put a bar across each door. (Peg's or Peleg's Grease Under the Nails gives advantage.) Three fewer will get out.
skillChecks.failure: There are too many windows and too little time. You do the old people's houses and hope.

skillChecks.success: Ellery Wyman has given everyone a key but has not given his own to anyone. He means to lock himself in alone, because he will not have a neighbor see him called. He will break the door down at the bell. (If someone is with him, he is held, and does not get out.)
skillChecks.failure: The First Selectman is doing what First Selectmen do. You cannot tell what he is thinking.

encounters: No fights: the island at its best, frightened and together
The gale (combat.json and dread.json isolation: no boat can run; the mail boat does not come on Wednesday)

acts.title: One Hour on the Shelf
acts.description: Wednesday 29 October, 4:45 to 6:30 a.m., run as a countdown in five-minute turns. 4:45: the Bar is a road; Galen Coombs's crew are already out on the Shelf's edge with lanterns, bringing up salt-sacks. 5:15: the Shelf is bare to the church; the church stands in a pool of black water knee-deep at its west front. 5:20: the bell begins, in open air, deafening, and every one of the blood who is not held walks; the answering bell in the Harbor makes the called stop and stand wherever they are, but it cannot stop this bell, which goes on ringing until the doors are opened or the water comes back over it, and called people standing still on the Shelf will drown standing. 5:30: Galen sets his charge on the west wall by the doors, eight sticks, a ten-minute fuse, and lights it unless he has been persuaded or stopped (Peleg's Sapper can pull it in one action with a Dexterity check DC 10; anyone else, DC 15, or cut the fuse with a knife, DC 12). 5:48: low water; the first grey of dawn. 6:00: the wind drops and backs; the tide turns, and comes back fast. 6:15: water over the Shelf's lower edge and running in the channels knee-deep. 6:25: over the church floor; waist-deep at the doors. 6:30: the Shelf is gone. Drawing the spikes: eight spikes, Athletics DC 14 with a crowbar for every two, one attempt per person per turn, two people can work at once; Heavy Work and the Longshoreman's strength give advantage; Shoulder to It helps. When the eighth spike is out and the doors are pulled open, the bell stops in the middle of a stroke, every called person wakes up wherever they stand, and the party see what is inside.
objectives: Get to the church doors and draw the eight spikes before 6:20
Stop Galen Coombs's charge, or make sure it does not bring the wall down on the doors
Get every one of the called, and Orpha Sprague, off the Shelf before the sea comes back
If you can, bring Esther Thurlow, Enoch Farr and Jotham Wyman out of the church

scenes.name: The Sea Goes Out
scenes.description: 4:45 to 5:20. The walk out: down the Bar in the dark and the wind, lanterns swinging, past the five Echo lights standing at the Bar's head, across the Point among the cellar holes, down the clay slope onto the Shelf. Weed underfoot like wet hair, pools, channels to wade, crabs scuttling from the lantern light, the smell of the bottom of the sea. Galen's lanterns out at the seaward edge. Then the church, rising up out of the dark in the lantern light, enormous, black and green, streaming, leaning, the boarded windows, the doors. Orpha Sprague, if she is with the party, walks the whole way on a cane and Peleg's arm and does not stop once. At 5:20 the bell. Ask every character for a fear check; then the called begin to come, out of the dark, behind them, across the Shelf, in nightclothes.
scenes.readAloud: You go out across the bottom of the sea. The weed is thick and slick as wet hair under your boots, and the lanterns make small gold rooms in the dark that slide over stone and pools and the white bellies of dead crabs. Everything is draining: water trickling, gurgling, running off the ledges in a hundred little streams, as if the whole Shelf were breathing out. Somewhere out on the seaward edge there are lanterns moving, and men's voices. And then the church is there, all at once, in front of you, much bigger than it looked from the shore: a wall of black weed and white barnacle forty feet high, its tower leaning over you against the stars, water pouring off its eaves, its windows boarded blind, and in the middle of it, under a broken pediment, two tall doors with iron across them. You are standing where the five men could not bring themselves to come. And above you, in the tower, very slowly, something in the dark begins to move. It is twenty past five. The bell rings. In the open air, for the first time in fifty-three years, it rings, and the sound comes down on you like the sea coming down on a beach.

skillChecks.success: The bell is so loud you feel it in your teeth, and behind you, across the Shelf, out of the dark, people are coming, walking, in nightgowns and stocking feet, their faces glad. You know what this is. You have read it. You go to the doors. (Knowing the bell's rules lowers this to DC 18.)
skillChecks.failure: It is the truth of it: the bell, the doors, the dead behind them, the living walking out to them in their nightclothes. Gain 1 Dread; on a natural 1, 2. Anyone of the blood who is not already awake and holding to something (Orpha with her lantern, Peleg or Dr. Thurlow with a crowbar in his hands and a friend beside him) must also make a Charisma save DC 15 or be called, and stand up and walk toward the doors like the others; an ally speaking their name gives a new save each round.

skillChecks.success: You take the dry line across the Shelf, the high ribs of granite between the pools, and reach the doors at 5:25 with time to spare. (Oren Pinkham's Fieldcraft and Mattie Grindle's knowledge of the bottom give this without a roll.)
skillChecks.failure: A channel deeper than it looked: everyone is wet to the waist, one lantern is lost, and you reach the doors at 5:35. (This is a good moment for the light to go out, once.)

skillChecks.success: At the church's west wall, ten yards to the left of the doors, two of Galen's men are packing something into a gap in the rotten clapboard, and Galen is uncoiling fuse. He has not seen you yet.
skillChecks.failure: The lanterns on the seaward edge are moving toward the church. You do not see where they stop.

scenes.name: The Doors
scenes.description: 5:25 to 6:15. The heart of the scenario. Run it in five-minute turns with the clock read aloud each turn. The doors: eight spikes, four Athletics checks DC 14 with crowbars (see Act description); Mattie Grindle, if Orpha has asked, draws the last spike while Orpha holds the lantern. Galen's charge: lit at 5:30 with a ten-minute fuse unless stopped; if it goes off at 5:40 while the doors are still shut, the west wall comes down across them (Dexterity save DC 13 for anyone within 20 ft, 3d6 bludgeoning, half on a success) and the doors are buried under a ton of wet timber: the party have failed tonight's work, the called still wake at the tide's return if they are got off the Shelf, and the doors must be reached by a diver in db-scenario-004; if the doors are already open, the blast instead brings the tower down and the bell falls out onto the Shelf, which will make it easier to raise in db-scenario-004. The called: nine (or fewer) of the blood walking out across the Shelf and gathering at the doors behind the party, swaying, glad, waiting, while the answering bell in the Harbor holds them still; if the party do not open the doors before 6:15 someone must lead each of them back by hand, one Athletics check DC 12 per person per turn, and the water is coming. Inside, once the doors open: the vestibule, the plaster names, Ardelia Vining on the rope, and the nave and its pews.
scenes.readAloud: The iron spikes are as thick as your thumb and crusted with rust and shell and weed, eight of them, driven through the doors into the old frame, and two iron straps across the whole, bolted. Somebody hammered these in with a sledge, by lantern light, one October fifty-three years ago, while the people inside listened. The crowbar's claw grates on the first spike and slips and grates again, and above your head the bell goes on and on, and behind you on the weed the called are gathering, one by one, out of the dark: a white-haired woman in a flannel nightgown, a big man in his underclothes with bare feet, Ellery Wyman in his trousers and braces with his face wet, standing in a half circle at your backs, swaying, smiling, patient, waiting for you to let them in.

skillChecks.success: The spike comes out of the frame with a shriek of iron and a gush of black water from the crack, and the next, and the strap's bolt shears. Two spikes drawn. (Four successes open the doors; the roughnecks' Heavy Work gives advantage, and two can work at once.)
skillChecks.failure: The spike moves an inch and stops. The crowbar slips and someone's knuckles are opened on the barnacles (1d4 slashing). The bell rings. Try again next turn.

skillChecks.success: If Galen's charge goes off: you are down on the weed with your arms over your head as the wall comes out in a roar of timber and water and smoke, and nothing hits you that you cannot get up from.
skillChecks.failure: If Galen's charge goes off: a beam comes down across your back and the world goes white. Take 3d6 bludgeoning damage, and you are prone in a foot of water with the tide coming.

skillChecks.success: The doors swing open. You see what is inside, and you do not look away, and you do not run. (Any character who has made this fear check against 'the truth of it' already this scene does not make it again.)
skillChecks.failure: The doors swing open, outward, on a rush of black water and a smell of fifty-three years, and in the lantern light there are people in the pews, sitting, and as you watch, all together, they stand up. Gain 1 Dread; a natural 1, 2. If you are at Dread 5, you flee, freeze or lash out (your choice), and someone had better be holding you.

scenes.name: The Sea Comes Home
scenes.description: When the doors open the bell stops in the middle of a stroke and every called person on the Shelf wakes up, cold and confused, four hundred yards from the shore with the tide turning. Inside, in the vestibule, a woman in a grey dress with her hands on a rope that is not there looks at the party and says 'Thank you' (Ardelia Vining; fear check DC 15; she does not attack, and the Sensitive can speak with her: CLUE F3). In the nave, the dead stand in their pews and turn toward the open doors, and do not come out; it is nearly sunrise, and they must be in the water by then (Drowned Ones are Water-Bound), and they will come ashore with the night's flood tide instead. The party have a few minutes for the vestibule plaster (CLUES D4, F4), for Esther and the other two taken of 1924 (carried out, one per strong person, Athletics DC 12 each turn on the way back), and for Galen's whisky in the vestry if anyone is fool enough. Then the sea comes home: from 6:00 the wind backs and drops and the water returns across the Shelf faster than a man can wade; at 6:15 it is knee-deep in the channels, at 6:25 waist-deep at the church. Every called person needs a hand to get back: Orpha must be carried. Galen's crew help if Galen has been brought round, and run for their dory if not. Let it be a desperate, splashing, freezing scramble up the clay slope onto the Point with the light coming grey over the sea, and the islanders on the Point reaching down to haul people up. Count heads at the top. If anyone was left, the GM should say so plainly.
scenes.readAloud: The bell stops. In the silence you can hear everything: the water running out of the church past your boots, a gull somewhere, someone behind you on the weed saying 'Where am I? Where am I?' in an old woman's voice, and the sea. The sea, coming back. You hear it before you see it: a low steady hiss like a kettle, from everywhere at once, and the pools at your feet are filling, and the channels you waded are running the other way, and in the grey light of the dawn the edge of the Shelf is gone under a line of white. In the church doorway, in the vestibule, a woman in a grey dress stands with her hands raised to a bell rope that is not there, and looks at you, and you see her face. She is not angry. She is very tired. 'Thank you,' she says. Behind her, in the dark, all down the nave, the people who were in the pews are standing, and turning, slowly, to look out at the open door, and the grey light, and the island.

skillChecks.success: You get your called person up off the weed and moving, an arm round them, toward the Point, through water rising to your knees and then your thighs, and up the clay slope where hands reach down for you. (Each called person, and Orpha, and each body carried, needs one success per turn for three turns from the church to the Point; the DC rises by 2 each turn after 6:10.)
skillChecks.failure: You go down in a channel together, under the cold water for a terrible second, and come up gasping, still holding on, a turn behind. A level of exhaustion if it happens twice.

skillChecks.success: Galen Coombs, staring at the spikes on the weed and the open doors and the people in the pews, understands, and starts shouting at his crew to drop the sacks and get the old folks up the slope. His four men and his dory make the difference: everyone gets off the Shelf. (Automatic if he was talked round in Act 1.)
skillChecks.failure: Galen's crew run for their dory with as many sacks as they can carry. Galen himself stays and helps, white-faced, without a word.

skillChecks.success: Ardelia Vining's face is only a tired woman's face. You meet her eyes, and nod, as you would to anyone who had thanked you, and turn and run for the shore.
skillChecks.failure: Her face is the last thing you see before you turn, and you will see it again tonight when you close your eyes. Gain 1 Dread.

encounters: The called: up to nine of the blood (fewer if the party helped lock the island in), who must be led off the Shelf by hand once the doors open; never hostile
Galen Coombs and four of his crew (Night Watchman statistics), at the charge: talk, a struggle on wet weed (brawling, combat.json; difficult terrain everywhere), or help

Ardelia Vining, the Ringer: use Bound Spirit statistics (CR 5) with these changes. Her bounds are the drowned church and the Shelf around it. On Carrow she is not vulnerable to salt (wrong rite); she is vulnerable only to her true name: 'Ardelia Vining' spoken to her makes her stop for a round. She never uses Take Hold on anyone opening the doors and never attacks the party unless someone attacks the church, the bell or her; Galen's charge-setters, if they persist after she has been seen, are the only likely targets of The House Obeys. She cannot be destroyed by violence, only laid by Rule 5.

The Drowned (Drowned One statistics, CR 1): the twenty-three of 1871 and the three of 1924, standing in their pews when the doors open; they do not leave the church before sunrise, and will not touch anyone who does not stand in the doorway to stop them. On Carrow the bell's rules replace the stat block's list of rules, except Water-Bound, which holds.

npcsInvolved.name: Miss Prudence Vining, 79
npcsInvolved.role: The Reverend Joel Vining's niece; keeper of his letters
npcsInvolved.description: Tall, thin, upright, steel spectacles, black bombazine, a schoolroom voice; taught Rockland's grammar school for forty-four years; lives on Middle Street with eleven clocks and a lap desk of letters.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To have her uncle believed, and his grief put to some use.

npcsInvolved.name: Willard Hosmer, 71
npcsInvolved.role: File clerk at the Rockland Mariner
npcsInvolved.description: Small, bald, cardigan, sleeve garters, the paper's memory since 1880. Delighted by anyone who wants old files and indignant at anyone who folds them.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To find you the thing you are looking for before you do.

npcsInvolved.name: Galen Coombs, 38
npcsInvolved.role: Rum-runner; the man with the dynamite
npcsInvolved.description: See db-scenario-001. In this scenario he is at his most dangerous and most frightened, and he can become an ally if he sees the spikes.
npcsInvolved.motivation: End the bell his way, recover $18,000 of whisky, and never be called like his aunt.

npcsInvolved.name: Arno Farr, 27
npcsInvolved.description: Thick, quiet, frightened, a Farr of the blood; has been inside the drowned church three times in the dress and will not go again.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Never to go back down there, and to tell someone what he saw.

npcsInvolved.name: Orpha Sprague, 73
npcsInvolved.description: See db-scenario-001. In this scenario she means to walk out to the church doors with her father's lantern.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To stand where she should have stood in 1871.

npcsInvolved.name: Ellery Wyman, 58
npcsInvolved.description: See db-scenario-001. In this scenario he organises the island's lock-in, locks himself in alone, and breaks his own door down at the bell.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To keep the island alive tonight, and not to be seen called by his neighbors.

npcsInvolved.name: Ardelia Vining (died 1871, aged 34)
npcsInvolved.role: The Ringer; the minister's wife who rang the bell for four hours
npcsInvolved.description: A slight woman in a grey dress and a nurse's apron, brown hair coming down, wet to the waist, hands raised to a bell rope. Very tired, very patient, not angry. Use Bound Spirit statistics with the changes in Act 3.
npcsInvolved.motivation: For someone to come. Then, to be named.

rewards.money: None from the island, which has nothing to give but its thanks: but every family whose called member was brought off the Shelf sends something, a quarter of beef, a knitted jersey, a barrel of salt herring, a jar of money, and Ellery Wyman tears up the party's account at the Store in front of everyone. Galen Coombs pays $200 to anyone who pulled one of his crew out of the water, and nothing to anyone who touched his charge. Merrymeeting Life, if Esther Thurlow's body is brought out, will pay $3,000 to Dr. Thurlow on Len Garrity's report.
items: Joel Vining's letter of March 1872, on loan from Miss Vining
Nehemiah Pinkham's 1871 logbook, or Oren's fair copy of the page
Two or more of the iron spikes from the church doors, which no islander will touch
A rubbing or a copy of the vestibule plaster names, if anyone thought to make one
Esther Thurlow, Enoch Farr and Jotham Wyman, if they were brought out, to be buried under their own names on Spruce Hill
Galen Coombs's chart of the Shelf, and his forty sticks, if he gives them up

twists: The party may go out to the church before the lowest tide: a diver in Galen's deep-sea dress can reach the vestry window at any low water, as Arno Farr did. It is terrifying and achieves nothing: the doors must be opened from outside, and from the vestry the diver sees only the backs of the doors and the dead in the pews. Let them try; it makes the Shelf on the 29th familiar and worse.

The doors open outward. When the eighth spike comes out, the weight of water still inside the church pushes them open by itself, with a rush that knocks anyone in front of them off their feet into the pool (Dexterity save DC 12 or prone and soaked).

On the night of Wednesday 29 October, at the flood tide around midnight, wet bare footprints come up out of the sea onto the Harbor beach and up the lanes to the doors of the five families' houses, and stop at every door with iron over it, and go on past it, and walk straight in through the one door in the Harbor without iron: the parsonage, which Kingsley Trask had painted in the summer and never put the spike back on. He wakes at two in the morning with the smell of the sea in his kitchen and water on the floor. That is the end of this scenario and the first sign of the next (CLUE E2, E3).

If the doors were buried by Galen's charge, the bell still stops at the tide's return (the Shelf is covered) and the called still wake, but nothing comes ashore that night, and on 13 November the bell will call two. The only way to the doors is now under the sea, in the dress, at night.
dmTips: The two weeks are for the truth; the hour is for courage. Let the players learn D, E and F in Act 1 and the Gale, so that by Wednesday morning they know exactly what they are walking into and why. The fear is better when they understand it.

Run the hour on the Shelf as a clock: say the time every turn. Write it on a card in the middle of the table. 5:20 the bell, 5:30 the fuse, 5:48 low water, 6:00 the turn, 6:15 the channels, 6:25 the church floor. Nothing ratchets dread like a number going down.
The called gathering silently behind the party at the doors, smiling, waiting to be let in, is the scenario's most frightening image. Hold it. Describe them one by one as they arrive.
Galen Coombs is not a villain. He is a frightened man with a bad idea and a box of dynamite. A party that gives him something better to do will have him at their side for the rest of the campaign.

Esther Thurlow in the pew is Dr. Thurlow's scene. Give him time. If he carries her out across the Shelf with the sea coming back, that is the campaign's best moment so far; do not hurry it with a roll if the player has something to say.

The dead standing up in their pews is the truth of the horror, and the GM should describe it once, briefly, and never in detail: shapes under weed, standing, turning toward the light. They are not attacking. They are looking at the open door.
Lines and veils: some players will not want the dead in the pews. Cut to the doors opening and Ardelia's 'Thank you' and the sea, and let the plaster names carry it.
